newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end slightly lower due to yen's weakness.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end slightly lower due to yen's weakness.

text.p: Key March Japanese government bond futures ended slightly lower on Thursday due to the yen's weakness versus the dollar.

The March was firm earlier, due to a fall in Tokyo share prices, but dipped into negative territory toward the close as the dollar edged close to 124 yen in afternoon trade, a trader for a trust bank's securities unit said.
Traders said concern about Japan's financial system was likely to persist, despite Nippon Credit Bank's denial on Wednesday of rumours about its financial health.
The March ended at 126.28 on Thursday, down slightly from Wednesday's 126.30. Turnover was 31,698 contracts.
On Wednesday morning, the March surged due to a steep fall in Nippon Credit Bank's (NCB) share prices and a rumour, later denied, that the bank would hold an emergency media briefing.

"In the markets, unsourced rumours such as the suggestion that our bank is practically on the verge of collapse are circulating and are prompting sales of our shares and debentures. Such rumours are totally groundless and our bank would like to declare that these rumours are not true," NCB said in a statement on Wednesday.
Despite such denials, financial system worries are likely to linger and provide support for JGBs, the trader for a trust bank's securities unit said.

"Finance Minister (Hiroshi) Mitsuzuka said there are no financial worries right now. These are just words, and seem to lack substance... The more reassurances we hear, the more the market worries," the trader said.
Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee on Thursday that he did not think any financial worries existed at present over the massive problem loans of Japanese financial institutions.

Mitsuzuka said that the government was backing financial institutions' efforts to get rid of the bad loans and to restructure their businesses, adding that the firms were well on their way towards solving the bad loan problem by 2001.
A trader for another trust bank's securities unit said JGBs were feeling impact from a fall in bank share prices, rather than from vague fears of the possible collapse of financial institutions.
"Worries about financial institutions had a direct impact on stocks... Bonds were bought yesterday because of the fall in share prices, not...on rumours about NCB," the trader said.
The benchmark 182nd JGB yield stood at 2.390 percent, up slightly from the previous day's 2.385 percent.
On Thursday, the Industrial Bank of Japan's January bank debentures were traded at 1.615 percent. Meanwhile, NCB's January bank debentures were offered at four percent.
A shift in benchmark status from the March to the June may take place next week or the week after, traders said.
Buying back pressure may support the March as it nears the benchmark shift, they said.
